title: 4 months as a "game director" — AI handled execution, I handled design. Workflow notes from PSYCHOBYL
author: AdJaded374
selftext:
Hey everyone,



Being honest up front because this sub deserves it: PSYCHOBYL is 4 months of solo work, but I didn't write the code, I didn't draw the art, and I didn't compose anything. I designed it. AI executed it. I'm essentially a non-coding game director who learned how to specify clearly and iterate fast.



What's actually mine:

\- The game design — mechanics, progression, balance, the prestige loop logic

\- The systems thinking — how idle + extraction + raids + bunker all interconnect

\- UI/UX design — every screen, every flow, every interaction I designed before AI built it

\- The Chernobyl 2084 + Genesis lore and tone

\- The decisions: what to cut, what to expand, what feels fun, what feels grindy

\- All quality control — every output gets reviewed, rejected, iterated on



What AI did:

\- All code (Cursor + Claude, but I specify behavior in plain English, read every line, push back when wrong)

\- All marketing visuals (generated, then I composite/edit/color-grade)

\- Most in-game art (batched, picked, edited to fit palette)

\- Refactors, debugging, even some balance math after I gave it the design constraints



The honest take after 4 months:

Design is the actual bottleneck now. AI builds whatever you tell it to build, in any direction, very fast. The bottleneck moved from "can I make this thing exist" to "do I actually know what should exist, and why?" Most of my day is system design on paper, then a 20-min spec to the AI, then 2 hours of testing the output and figuring out what was off about my spec.



What I learned:

\- AI's first pass at game systems is almost always shallow. The work is in iterating the spec until the output matches what you actually wanted.

\- A coherent design vision is the unifying force. AI doesn't naturally produce a "game that feels like one thing" — that's your job.

\- Quality control is exhausting and non-delegatable. You can't ship raw AI output.



Question for the community:

For those of you doing similar director-style workflows: how do you write specs that minimize iteration count? I'm still doing 3-4 rounds per non-trivial feature and I feel like I should be at 1-2.



Steam page for context: [https://store.steampowered.com/app/4514090/PSYCHOBYL/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4514090/PSYCHOBYL/)



Happy to talk specifics about any of it.

comments.author: zenith4eva
comments.body: Awesome stuff. Is there a game engine that you used such as Unity or godot?

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Thanks! Actually no — I went with a web-based stack: Electron + React + TypeScript. PSYCHOBYL is essentially a packaged web app that runs as a native Windows executable on Steam.



For an idle/turn-based RPG with mostly UI-driven gameplay and no real-time 3D, this stack is way faster to iterate on than Unity. I get hot reload, browser dev tools, and CSS for animations. Trade-off: I'd never use this for an FPS or anything physics-heavy.

comments.author: DegTrader
comments.body: So, we've officially moved from 'I spent 5 years in a basement learning C++' to 'I spent 5 hours on a caffeine-fueled prompting bender.' Truly, the future is just professional editing.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: Look up Skyebrows on youtube.  Makes AI music + music videos.  He's the director and editor.  And it is really good.  So there are skills that must be developed, but they are more the artistic vision skills than the drudging hard work stuff.

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Fair shot, and honestly somewhat true. The "5 years of C++" path used to be the only path, and there's a real argument that something is lost when execution gets fast.



But the way I think about it: AI moved the hard work from "can I make this exist" to "do I actually know what should exist, and why?" My day is 60% design and decision-making, not prompting. The bottleneck just shifted upstream.



Not arguing it's the same thing — just that "professional editing" might be underselling it a bit. Both paths produce games. Some good, some slop. Same as it ever was.

replies.author: hongkong_97
replies.body: Main issue is you claim you're a game director. More like a designer that prompts

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Fair pushback. "Director" was probably the wrong word choice on my part. "Designer who prompts" is honestly more accurate to the day to day. The director framing implies a level of orchestration and team coordination that doesn't really apply when it's just you and an LLM.



Maybe the better framing is: someone whose job moved from execution to specification. Still solo dev, still doing all the design work, but the "what should this look/feel/behave like" part is now where I spend my time, and the "make it exist in code/pixels" part is mostly delegated.



Words for this role are still being invented. "Director" oversells it. "Prompter" undersells it. Probably the right term hasn't landed yet.

replies.author: hongkong_97
replies.body: Yea, you're not directing anything. Kojima is a game director.

replies.author: dx0ne
replies.body:
Given state of nonAi games, especially in recent years, players didn't benefit much from "hard C++ way". Designs also lacked because adding new features and iteration costed a lot. Now prototypes are relatively free. Feature doesn't fit? Cut it without regrets.
Yours is greate exaple of rhings to come. And if someone has prior technical knowledge it would multiply even more.

But as tou said you still need ideas. Having camera in a phone doesn't make everybody Spilberg.

You stil need great ideas. Execution just got faster and cheaper.

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body: Spielberg/camera analogy is perfect, exactly the framing I've been struggling to put into words. Going to steal it. The "you still need great ideas" part is what I want people to take away. Thanks for the thoughtful comment.

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
Cream of the slop right here.  I would point all people who are making games using AI to this as their benchmark.  

I think if you could perfectly communicate your game idea, fully fleshed out, the first time, the AI has a high likelyhood of outputting that very thing.  The problem is thats damn near impossible to do.  First, our idea starts off pretty vague, more feeling than minute detail with specific systems and how they interact.  Second, our ability to communicate ideas with crystal clarity isn't all that good.  Historically, it has taken a book for an author to convey an idea decently well to other humans.  Often not all that well.  

For me, every time we fine tune the design idea, I have the AI either create or update a design doc, an MD for me.  I want to have a collection of documents that together communicate the exact game I am building.  That way I can upload those docs to another AI if needed and have their contextual "understanding" of the vision be correct.  or correct enough to start building.  Also, I want to use those docs to onboard another joining the project.

replies.author: Will_X_Intent
replies.body: What was your process for creating the video, if I may ask?

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Really appreciate this — and your design doc workflow point is spot on. I've been doing a lighter version of this (a single living "vision doc" markdown I keep updating), but having multiple structured docs that another AI could parse and "onboard" from is a much sharper version of the idea. Going to adopt that.



On the trailer process — actually pretty simple:



1. Just played the game and took screen recordings of the moments I wanted (raid scenes, hideout flows, menus)

2. Cut and edited everything in CapCut — picked the strongest moments, paced the cuts, added transitions between scenes

3. Music: composed in Suno AI — generated my own track to fit the Chernobyl/idle atmosphere



That's it. No DaVinci, no fancy color grading, no AI B-roll. Solo dev pragmatism — CapCut + Suno gets you 80% of the way there if you've got a clear vision of the tone you want.



Honestly the music selection was where I spent the most time. Suno lets you iterate on prompts until you get something that fits, but knowing when a track "fits" the game's emotional tone is the actual skill. I went through maybe 30-40 generations before settling on the one in the trailer.

comments.author: MrBearmode
comments.body: Looks really good. Nice job. Do you mind explaining your workflow for the art and UI?

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Sure! Quick breakdown:



**Art workflow:**

\- Marketing visuals (Steam capsules, etc.): generate with image models → bring into Pillow (Python) → composite, color-grade to match palette, sharpen, add brand elements (atom logo + text overlay via code)

\- In-game enemy/item art: batch generate 4-8 variants per asset → pick the closest → edit in image editor to fix details and match the toxic-green/charcoal palette I've locked in

\- Brand assets (atom logo, capsule typography): hand-coded in SVG + Pillow filters — needed exact pixel control



**UI workflow:**

\- Every screen designed on paper or Figma first (wireframe + flow)

\- Then I write a spec describing layout, state, interactions

\- AI implements the React/TSX component

\- I review, refactor, polish in CSS until the feel is right

\- Iteration count is usually 2-3 rounds per non-trivial screen



The thing that makes it not look "AI dumped" is the palette discipline — everything goes through the same color/tone pass before it ships.

comments.author: The_Great_Pains
comments.body: I've always wanted to try something like this.  How do you make that awesome imagery?  Is everything AI?

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
Most of the marketing imagery is AI-generated, but every single piece gets at least 2-3 manual passes — composite, recolor to match palette, sharpen, add brand overlays (the atom logo + text are hand-coded). Raw AI outputs never make it into the final.



If you want to try something similar, the biggest unlock for me was locking in a fixed color palette early. Everything you generate gets dragged toward that palette in post-processing, and suddenly your assets look like they belong to one game instead of 50 different vibes.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Glad to see a project someone actually put time and effort into and it shows.

One tip I wanted to add to your learning list that I've had massive success with when coding complex systems was: Build content creation tools with the AI. For instance if you have an equipment system, one of the first things I'd do is work with AI to build a tool that lets me add equipment manually into the game, but that also provides a back-end method for the AI to easily do the same following a set of derived instructions. Also a method for easily viewing/editing all the assets already part of the system. This is how major game studios do things (see Bethesda's Creation Kit -- though often they're just internal tools.)

Agreed with everything else you've said, and they mirror my own findings. Keep at it.

replies.author: AdJaded374
replies.body:
That’s a really great tip, and it’s something I’ve been doing to some extent without realizing it, but I should actually be doing it more consciously. I created a small JSON-based content editor for enemies, items, and loot, but you’re right—making this bidirectional (so the AI can also generate content by following the same schema) will speed up my process of adding new gear by a factor of 10.



After the demo launch, I could formalize this as a “content kit.” The comparison to the Creation Kit sparked something in me—this is exactly the model I need to work on.



Thanks for your thoughtful comment; this is exactly the kind of feedback I came here for.
